fidelity_vs_completeness_conflict.note: GameCube via Dolphin is the cleanest high-fidelity route for the main game, but the PS2/PSP linked route has exclusive arenas and cars not available on GameCube or Xbox.

entries.title: Crash Team Racing Nitro-Fueled

primary.version: Xbox One X Enhanced version on Xbox One X or Series X
primary.why: public release references lists Nitro-Fueled on PlayStation 4, Xbox One, and Nintendo Switch. Technical reporting lists both Xbox One X and PS4 Pro at 2560x1440 and 30fps, but the Xbox listing also carries HDR10 and Xbox One X Enhanced support, making it the strongest non-exclusive high-fidelity route. PS4 has exclusive retro content, so it is kept as a secondary content check rather than replacing the Xbox primary.
primary.how_to_play: Use the updated Xbox One version on Xbox One X or Series X for the main Nitro-Fueled route. Then run the PS4 version to capture Retro Stadium plus the PS4-exclusive retro skins/karts if the archive wants every exclusive item.

secondary.why: PS4 has exclusive retro content: retro skins and karts for Crash, Coco, and Cortex, plus a retro track/Retro Stadium. Play this version for that exclusive track and those cosmetics after the primary route.

all_releases.fidelity: PS4 Pro reaches the same reported 2560x1440/30fps class as Xbox One X, and PS4 has exclusive retro content.
all_releases.reason: Secondary because the PS4 version uniquely includes retro skins/karts and a retro track, but Xbox One X/Series is the higher-fidelity primary due to HDR/Xbox One X Enhanced support.

all_releases.fidelity: Xbox One X Enhanced, HDR10-capable route; reported 2560x1440 at 30fps on Xbox One X and playable on Series X/S through Xbox compatibility.
all_releases.reason: Primary because it matches the top reported resolution/framerate tier and has Xbox One X Enhanced/HDR flags, while no exclusive gameplay content is missing except PS4-only retro content handled separately.

all_releases.fidelity: Portable/docked Switch release; reported 720p docked and about 480p handheld with the same core game content.
all_releases.reason: Skip for main archive capture because it is technically lower fidelity and no exclusive content was sourced.

fidelity_vs_completeness_conflict.note: Xbox One X/Series is the highest-fidelity primary because of 1440p-class output plus HDR/Xbox One X Enhanced support, but PS4 has exclusive retro content. Archive the PS4 Retro Stadium/retro cosmetics separately.

entries.definitive_edition: No PC or native next-gen definitive edition was released. The Nitros Oxide Edition is a content bundle/early-unlock package with exclusive cosmetics, not a different technical version.
entries.remaster_caveats: Nitro-Fueled remakes the 1999 Crash Team Racing and adds Crash Nitro Kart/post-launch material, but it should remain separate from the original Crash Team Racing entry. Online features and Wumpa Coin/in-game purchase availability can change.

emulation.emulator: None for primary; use native Xbox hardware/backward compatibility.
emulation.notes: No PC version exists. Use Xbox One X or Series X/S for the primary capture, PS4/PS4 Pro for Retro Stadium and retro cosmetics, and Switch only for portability comparison.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Xbox One X Enhanced / Xbox Series compatibility route at the top console fidelity tier.

entries.title: Crash Team Rumble

primary.why: public release references and Activision list Crash Team Rumble on PS4, PS5, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X/S. It is an online-only 4v4 cross-platform game, and the Xbox listing explicitly marks the title Optimized for Xbox Series X|S with Smart Delivery. No platform-exclusive gameplay content was sourced, so Xbox Series X is the cleanest high-fidelity/current-console route.
primary.how_to_play: Use the Xbox Series X|S version with an Activision account and active console online subscription. Verify server status before capture because the game is online-required and its final content update was March 4, 2024.

all_releases.fidelity: PS4 cross-gen release; PlayStation page lists online play required and PS4 Pro Enhanced support.
all_releases.reason: Skip because it has no sourced exclusive gameplay content versus current-gen versions and is lower priority than PS5/Xbox Series for fidelity.

all_releases.fidelity: Native PS5 release with DualSense vibration support and online play required.
all_releases.reason: Skip because no PS5-exclusive maps, characters, or modes were sourced; DualSense support is an input feature, not archive-exclusive game content.

all_releases.fidelity: Xbox One cross-gen release sharing the same online service and cross-platform pool.
all_releases.reason: Skip because it has no sourced exclusive content and lower fidelity than the Xbox Series route.

all_releases.fidelity: Optimized for Xbox Series X|S with Smart Delivery; official Xbox listing supports online multiplayer and cross-gen/cross-platform capabilities.
all_releases.reason: Primary because it is a current-gen optimized release with no sourced content loss versus other platforms.

fidelity_vs_completeness_conflict.note: No platform-exclusive gameplay content was sourced. The meaningful conflict is preservation rather than content: the game requires online services and an Activision account.

entries.definitive_edition: No offline or expanded definitive edition was released. After the March 4, 2024 final content update, the core game remained live with a free 500-tier battle pass containing prior seasonal/event rewards, but the experience still depends on online services.
entries.remaster_caveats: Not a remaster. It is a live-service-style multiplayer spin-off; final content support ended in 2024 and server availability must be checked before any archive capture.

emulation.notes: Use native Xbox Series X|S or PS5 hardware. Emulation is not practical because the game is online-required and server-dependent.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Native current-gen console release, with Xbox Series X|S selected for the optimized primary route.

entries.title: Crash Twinsanity

primary.version: Original Xbox release via xemu or original Xbox hardware
primary.why: public release references lists the console game on PlayStation 2 and Xbox. The Xbox version supports 480p progressive scan, widescreen, and Dolby Digital, while the PS2 version lists widescreen but not progressive scan; GameSpot also found the PS2 frame-rate problems more persistent than Xbox. The Xbox release is therefore the best-fidelity complete console route, with PS2 only needed for comparison or the Action Pack compilation.
primary.how_to_play: Use the Xbox version on original Xbox hardware, or xemu if the current compatibility report still holds. Avoid Xbox 360 backward compatibility for final capture unless specifically testing it, because community version notes report notable slowdowns there.

all_releases.fidelity: Original PS2 release; widescreen-capable but no Moby-listed progressive scan, and reviews report more persistent frame-rate issues than Xbox.
all_releases.reason: Skip because no PS2-exclusive story, levels, characters, or modes were sourced; the later Crash Bandicoot Action Pack is a PS2 compilation, not new game content.

all_releases.fidelity: Original Xbox release with 480p progressive scan, widescreen, Dolby Digital, and less persistent frame-rate criticism than PS2.
all_releases.reason: Primary because it is the highest-fidelity complete console release and has no sourced content loss versus PS2.

fidelity_vs_completeness_conflict.note: No exclusive content split was sourced between PS2 and Xbox. Xbox is the fidelity pick; PS2 is useful only for comparison or if xemu/original Xbox capture has issues.

entries.definitive_edition: No remaster or definitive edition. Crash Bandicoot Action Pack is a three-disc PlayStation 2 bundle containing the PS2 release, not a technically improved version.
entries.remaster_caveats: A planned GameCube version was cancelled; do not invent it as a shipped release. The J2ME Crash Twinsanity and Crash Twinsanity 3D mobile games are separate entries with different gameplay.

emulation.emulator: xemu for the Xbox primary; PCSX2 as a PS2 fallback/comparison route.
emulation.notes: xemu currently reports no known issues for Crash Twinsanity, but original Xbox emulation should still be play-tested for capture. Xbox 360 backward compatibility is documented as slowdown-prone in community version notes.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Original Xbox 480p progressive/widescreen/Dolby route, captured through native hardware or xemu.

entries.title: Crash Twinsanity 3D

primary.why: public release references lists Crash Twinsanity 3D as a J2ME release published by Vivendi Games Mobile/Wonderphone and developed by Kuju. It is explicitly not the same as the 2D mobile Crash Twinsanity: this version is a behind-view 3D runner/platformer without the Crash-and-Cortex team-up of the console and 2D mobile games. public release references dates it to 2005; contemporary launch summaries describe a late-2004 Vodafone 3G rollout, so the archive should note the date conflict but keep Moby as the release-year anchor.
primary.how_to_play: Run the J2ME build in KEmulator nnmod or another J2ME emulator with 3D support, and document the handset/resolution profile used. Test loading and collision-sensitive sections before final capture.

all_releases.fidelity: Original Java ME 3D mobile release for 3G/Java handsets; best preserved through a J2ME emulator with 3D support.
all_releases.reason: Primary because it is the only shipped platform sourced for this distinct 3D mobile game.

fidelity_vs_completeness_conflict.note: Only the J2ME/mobile release is sourced. The conflict is emulator accuracy and handset profile selection, not platform content.

entries.definitive_edition: No definitive edition or later remaster was found.
entries.remaster_caveats: Do not confuse this with the console Crash Twinsanity or the 2D J2ME Crash Twinsanity. It has separate behind-view 3D mobile gameplay and no Cortex team-up according to public release references.

emulation.emulator: KEmulator nnmod or J2ME Loader/JL-Mod style tooling
emulation.notes: Use a J2ME emulator that supports 3D APIs. KEmulator nnmod advertises a hardware-accelerated 3D engine and broad OEM API support; J2ME Loader is another useful baseline for many Java ME games.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Original J2ME 3D handset rendering, scaled/captured through emulator.

entries.title: Crash Twinsanity Mobile

primary.why: public release references lists the mobile Crash Twinsanity as a November 6, 2004 J2ME game published by Wonderphone and developed by Kaolink. Its design is not a port of the full console game: it is a 2D side-view mobile game built around the Doc Amok-style task of protecting Cortex through six levels. No other shipped platform was sourced.
primary.how_to_play: Use the J2ME build in J2ME Loader or KEmulator, choose the matching handset resolution/profile, and capture all six levels. Keep Crash Twinsanity 3D separate because it is a different mobile game.

all_releases.fidelity: Original 2D Java ME mobile release; best preserved through J2ME emulation with the correct handset resolution.
all_releases.reason: Primary because it is the only sourced platform for this distinct mobile game.

fidelity_vs_completeness_conflict.note: Only the J2ME release is sourced. Completeness depends on using a matching handset build/profile, not choosing among ports.

entries.definitive_edition: No definitive edition or later remaster was found.
entries.remaster_caveats: Do not merge this with the console Crash Twinsanity or Crash Twinsanity 3D. public release references treats the J2ME game as a separate mobile title with different side-view gameplay.

emulation.notes: J2ME Loader supports most 2D games with per-application settings and scaling; KEmulator is a PC-oriented alternative for Java mobile capture.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Original J2ME 2D handset rendering, scaled/captured through emulator.

entries.title: Cyberpunk 2077

primary.version: Cyberpunk 2077: Ultimate Edition / base game plus Phantom Liberty, latest PC patch
primary.why: Windows is the highest-fidelity and most complete route: public release references lists the base game first on Windows, and the Phantom Liberty/Ultimate bundle includes the expansion; PC also supports the full current patch line, Ray Tracing: Overdrive/path tracing, DLSS Ray Reconstruction, and scalable settings beyond console targets. Last-gen PS4/Xbox One and Stadia miss Phantom Liberty and later 2.x-era content support, while current consoles, Mac, and Switch 2 do not add exclusive story or mission content over PC.
primary.how_to_play: Use the Windows version updated to the latest patch, with Phantom Liberty installed. For best capture, use a high-end RTX PC, enable Ray Tracing: Overdrive/path tracing and Ray Reconstruction if performance allows, and document DLSS/upscaling, frame generation, HDR, mods, and patch number.

entries.title: Demon's Souls

primary.version: Original PlayStation 3 release via RPCS3 or PS3 hardware
primary.why: This entry is for FromSoftware's 2009 original, not the 2020 remake. public release references lists the shipped game on PlayStation 3 only. RPCS3 is the best high-fidelity preservation route because it can run the PS3 game with higher internal resolution and optional FPS/unblur patches while preserving the original content; original PS3 hardware remains the authenticity fallback.
primary.how_to_play: Use RPCS3 for high-resolution capture of the PS3 release, documenting any patches such as Unlock FPS or motion-blur removal. Use real PS3 hardware when testing original timing or private-server online behavior.

all_releases.fidelity: Only shipped platform for the original game; best preserved today either on PS3 hardware or through RPCS3 with optional enhancement patches.
all_releases.reason: Primary because this is the actual original release. The PS5 remake is a separate 2020 entry, not a replacement for the original-route archive.

fidelity_vs_completeness_conflict.note: The original has only one shipped platform. RPCS3 can raise fidelity, while PS3 hardware best represents launch-era behavior. The remake is deliberately handled as a separate title.

entries.definitive_edition: No definitive edition of the original. Use the PlayStation 3 version, preferably via RPCS3 for high-fidelity original-content capture.
entries.remaster_caveats: Do not conflate the 2020 Bluepoint/Japan Studio remake with the 2009 FromSoftware original. Official PS3 servers shut down February 28, 2018; The Archstones is an unofficial preservation/private-server option, not the original official service.

emulation.notes: RPCS3 marks Demons Souls playable and exposes game patches such as Unlock FPS, Skip Intro Videos, and Disable Motion Blur. The Archstones can restore online-style behavior through a private server for PS3/RPCS3, but it is unofficial.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Original PS3 content rendered at high internal resolution and optionally 60fps through RPCS3.

entries.title: Hey You, Pikachu!

primary.version: Original cartridge with same-region Voice Recognition Unit and microphone

NintendoWiki notes that the VRU is required for Hey You, Pikachu!, was bundled with the game, and was never released in PAL regions, so original NTSC hardware with the matching VRU is the most faithful complete route.
primary.how_to_play: Use an original NTSC-J or NTSC-U Nintendo 64 cartridge, a same-region Nintendo 64 console, and the matching VRU/microphone plugged into controller port 4. Use the analog stick for navigation and voice commands for Pikachu; avoid PAL assumptions because the VRU was not released there.

all_releases.fidelity: Original N64 release built around the bundled Voice Recognition Unit and microphone; Japanese release is Pikachu Genki Dechū, followed by the North American Hey You, Pikachu! release.
all_releases.reason: This is the only sourced platform release and the only complete route because the VRU is required for the core interaction model.

fidelity_vs_completeness_conflict.note: No alternate platform or remaster is sourced. The hardware requirement is part of the complete original experience rather than a version tradeoff.

entries.remaster_caveats: No Virtual Console, Switch Online, remake, or remaster release is sourced. Pokémon Channel has similar Pikachu-care themes but is a separate GameCube game, not a rerelease or replacement. The VRU is region-sensitive and NintendoWiki states it was never released in PAL regions.

emulation.notes: Because voice recognition hardware is required and region-specific, emulator capture should only be used after verifying VRU/microphone support for the specific emulator and ROM region. Original hardware remains the primary archive route.

primary.why: Pokemon Colosseum shipped on GameCube, and the North American route is the best main archive path because it provides the English story mode plus the source-backed Jirachi bonus disc. Japanese bonus-disc Celebi/Pikachu content is real but belongs to a secondary regional cleanup path.
primary.how_to_play: Play the North American GameCube disc on GameCube hardware, backward-compatible Wii, or Dolphin for capture. If covering transfer extras, use the North American bonus disc with Ruby/Sapphire and a GameCube-GBA link cable, then sample the Japanese bonus disc separately for Celebi/Pikachu transfer content.

secondary.exclusive_content: Japanese bonus disc downloads Celebi and Pikachu, while the North American bonus disc downloads Jirachi.
secondary.what_to_play: Use the Japanese bonus disc only for the Celebi/Pikachu transfer content after the North American main route.
secondary.why: Approved sources identify different bonus-disc transfer gifts by region; this is supplemental content, not a separate main story route.

all_releases.fidelity: Original Japanese GameCube release; Japanese bonus disc includes Celebi and Pikachu downloads.
all_releases.reason: secondary: required only for the Japanese bonus-disc transfer gifts after the English main run.

all_releases.fidelity: Original English GameCube release; North American pre-order bonus disc includes Jirachi transfer to Ruby/Sapphire.
all_releases.reason: primary: English main route plus source-backed Jirachi bonus-disc content.

all_releases.fidelity: PAL GameCube release with the same core story/battle game.
all_releases.reason: skip: approved sources note the PAL market did not receive the bonus disc; use only for PAL localization or hardware comparison.

fidelity_vs_completeness_conflict.note: North America is the best English main route with Jirachi bonus content, while Japan has different bonus-disc transfer gifts; full event-transfer coverage requires both regional bonus discs.

entries.definitive_edition: North American GameCube release with bonus disc for the main route; Japanese bonus disc as secondary
entries.remaster_caveats: No currently available modern port is listed in the approved sources used here. Public sources indicate a Nintendo Classics release is expected, but until it is actually available and bonus-disc behavior is known, original GameCube remains the archive route.

emulation.emulator: GameCube hardware, backward-compatible Wii, or Dolphin

emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Original GameCube presentation; emulator upscaling available for capture, with transfer extras best verified on hardware.

primary.version: 2021 MAGES remake, standalone or bundled with the other Famicom Detective Club remake
primary.why: Wikipedia documents the original Famicom Detective Club case and the 2021 Nintendo Switch remake, while Nintendo describes the Switch release as modernized with updated visuals, fully voiced cutscenes, and English on-screen text. The Switch remake is therefore the highest-fidelity and most accessible complete route.
primary.how_to_play: Play the official Nintendo Switch release, standalone or from the two-game bundle. Use docked output for clean capture, English on-screen text, and Japanese voiceover; keep Famicom/GBA/Virtual Console versions only for historical comparison.

summary: Famicom Disk System golf releases from Nintendo and HAL, with Disk Fax contest prize disks treated as secondary exclusive-course content.

entries.title: Family Computer Golf: Japan Course

primary.version: Original blue-disk Golf: Japan Course release
primary.why: public release references lists Golf: Japan Course as a February 21, 1987 NES/Famicom Disk System release developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo, with Famicom Disk System media. There is no sourced later platform or remaster, so the highest-fidelity main route is a clean dump of the original blue disk in accurate FDS emulation. The gold prize disks add exclusive harder courses, but they replace the course content rather than serving as the normal main version.
primary.how_to_play: Use a legally dumped original Family Computer Golf: Japan Course blue disk in an accurate Famicom Disk System emulator such as Mesen or ares. Preserve 4:3, original timing, and disk-write/save behavior; after the main retail 18-hole route, play the Professional Course and Champions' Course prize disks only as secondary exclusive-course mop-ups if verified copies/dumps are available.

secondary.platform: Family Computer Disk System - Golf: Japan Course (Professional Course)
secondary.exclusive_content: Gold-disk prize version with a harder alternate 18-hole course, given to tournament runners-up.
secondary.what_to_play: Play the Professional Course holes as a secondary run after completing or sampling the retail Japan Course.
secondary.why: Super Mario Wiki documents Professional Course as a special Golf: Japan Course release on FDS with more difficult holes, and Family Computer Disk System coverage identifies it as one of the gold-disk tournament prizes.

secondary.platform: Family Computer Disk System - Golf: Japan Course (Champions' Course)
secondary.exclusive_content: Very rare gold-disk prize version for top tournament winners with a different, harder course layout; public preservation appears incomplete.
secondary.what_to_play: Treat as an archive target and play only if a verified dump or physical capture becomes available; otherwise document its missing/inaccessible status.
secondary.why: Super Mario Wiki documents Champions' Course as a separate tournament prize for 100 winners and notes that the game has not been dumped, so it is real exclusive content but not reliably playable today.

all_releases.fidelity: Original FDS blue-disk release; best fidelity comes from accurate FDS emulation or clean original-hardware capture because no remaster or port is sourced.
all_releases.reason: primary: public release references and Mario Wiki list only the Famicom Disk System/NES platform for the retail Japan Course, making this the required main playthrough for the standard course.

all_releases.platform: Family Computer Disk System - Professional Course prize disk
all_releases.fidelity: Same FDS-era engine and presentation as retail, but with a harder alternate course distributed on a gold disk.
all_releases.reason: secondary: exclusive alternate course content not present on the retail Japan Course blue disk; play only for that course, not as the main route.

all_releases.platform: Family Computer Disk System - Champions' Course prize disk
all_releases.fidelity: Same FDS-era engine and presentation, but tied to an extremely scarce tournament-winner course; public dump/access is not confirmed.
all_releases.reason: secondary: exclusive harder course content, but current public preservation is incomplete, so this is a documentation/play-if-accessible target.

fidelity_vs_completeness_conflict.note: There is no platform fidelity split, but the normal retail blue disk is not content-complete because the Professional Course and Champions' Course prize disks contain exclusive harder course layouts. Primary stays on the retail disk; secondary covers the prize courses.

entries.definitive_edition: Original Family Computer Disk System blue disk, plus gold-disk prize courses as secondary content
entries.remaster_caveats: No sourced remaster, port, or official modern reissue was found. The Disk Fax tournament/service features are defunct, and Champions' Course is documented as not publicly dumped, so full archival completeness may require rare physical access.

emulation.emulator: Mesen or ares with Famicom Disk System support
emulation.notes: Use accurate FDS emulation with the BIOS and legal disk dumps; verify save/disk-write behavior because the original used Disk Fax score data. Preserve 4:3 and avoid enhancement filters for archival capture.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Accurate FDS emulation or clean original-hardware RGB/capture

entries.title: Family Computer Golf: U.S. Course

primary.version: Original blue-disk Golf: U.S. Course release
primary.why: public release references lists Golf: US Course, also known as Family Computer Golf: U.S. Course, as a June 14, 1987 NES/Famicom Disk System release by HAL Laboratory and Nintendo, and describes it as the companion to Japan Course with Disk Fax compatibility. No later platform or remaster is sourced, so accurate FDS emulation of the retail blue disk is the primary route; the gold Golf: Special Course prize disk is secondary because it adds a harder special course rather than replacing the normal U.S. Course.
primary.how_to_play: Use a legally dumped Golf: U.S. Course blue disk in Mesen or ares with Famicom Disk System support. Preserve 4:3 and original timing; after the retail U.S. Course route, play Golf: Special Course only as a secondary exclusive-course run if a verified copy/dump is available.

secondary.platform: Family Computer Disk System - Golf: Special Course
secondary.exclusive_content: Gold-disk prize version of Golf: U.S. Course with a harder Special Course and a hidden female character unlock route.
secondary.what_to_play: Play the Special Course after the retail U.S. Course; optionally document the hidden character condition if using a verified dump/copy.
secondary.why: Super Mario Wiki documents Golf: Special Course as a special Golf: U.S. Course release distributed as a prize, with its harder course and hidden character details.

all_releases.fidelity: Original FDS blue-disk release; best available fidelity is accurate FDS emulation or clean original-hardware capture because no remaster or port is sourced.
all_releases.reason: primary: public release references and Mario Wiki list the retail U.S. Course on Famicom Disk System/NES, making it the normal complete main course route.

all_releases.platform: Family Computer Disk System - Golf: Special Course prize disk
all_releases.fidelity: Same FDS-era engine and presentation as U.S. Course, but with a harder special course on a gold prize disk.
all_releases.reason: secondary: exclusive special-course content not present on the retail U.S. Course blue disk; play as a content mop-up only.

fidelity_vs_completeness_conflict.note: There is no higher-fidelity platform alternative, but content completeness requires the Golf: Special Course prize disk after the retail U.S. Course because it contains a harder special course not in the primary.

entries.definitive_edition: Original Family Computer Disk System blue disk, plus Golf: Special Course as secondary content
entries.remaster_caveats: No sourced remaster, port, or official modern reissue was found. Disk Fax contest functionality is defunct, and the Special Course gold disk was a limited prize item rather than a normal retail release.

emulation.emulator: Mesen or ares with Famicom Disk System support
emulation.notes: Use accurate FDS emulation with a legal disk dump and BIOS. Preserve the original 4:3 presentation and verify save/disk-write behavior because the retail disk was designed around Disk Fax score submission.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Accurate FDS emulation or clean original-hardware RGB/capture
